newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu, once a master player, seeks a last ace.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu, once a master player, seeks a last ace.

text.p: During his 32 years in power in Zaire, President Mobutu Sese Seko has always had an ace card up his sleeve when the going was tough.
If he has one now, as rebels press against the shrinking enclave he still claims to control, Mobutu needs to produce it fast.
The collapse of peace talks, the defeat of his ragged army and the steady assault on his health from cancer have conspired to leave Mobutu virtually defenceless against Laurent Kabila's rebels.
One insult never thrown at the 66-year-old marshall is cowardice and the presidential camp, at the risk of flirting with surrealism, is still insisting Mobutu should remain in office until elections.

A foreign member of the president's public relations team insisted on Monday that the army, miraculously invigorated, had recaptured Kikwit, the strategic town 400 km (250 miles) east of Kinshasa taken by Kabila last week.

But diplomatic and other sources in contact with Kikwit dismissed the claim and said the frontline was close to the strategic Kwango River bridge less than 200 km (125 miles) from the excited and expectant city of five million people.
Nor is there any proof that Jonas Savimbi, leader of Angola's former UNITA rebels and a close ally of Mobutu's, has decided to throw troops into Zaire against the rebels.
Savimbi has every reason to fear a Zaire led by Kabila, who has received extensive military and political support from the Angolan government, according to senior diplomatic sources.

If Mobutu's last loyalists in the presidential guard, many of whom are from his minority Ngbandi ethnic group, ever decide to make a genuine last stand the location has to be the Kwango bridge, diplomatic sources said.

Military and diplomatic sources say Mobutu's guard, once trained by Israel, is well armed and supplied. What is uncertain is whether it has the stomach for a Battle of Kinshasa, defending a president who controls a tiny part of Africa's third largest country.

If there is no resistance and the loyalists flee across the Zaire River into neighbouring Congo, the danger feared by all residents rich or poor is an outbreak of mass looting before Kabila's rebels arrive.
Kinshasa was devastated by army-led looting in 1991 and 1993 but there was almost no violence against foreigners and Mobutu regained control after a few days.
This time, there will be no authority in charge until the rebels turn up and diplomats fear a settling of personal scores as well as generalised pillaging by the dirt-poor populace.

Foreign governments are repeating prior warnings to their nationals to leave Zaire at once. Waiting in Congo, as well as nearby in Gabon and off the Central African coast, is a powerful military presence sent weeks ago by the United States, Belgium, France and Britain. It has swollen to at least 4,000 fighting troops, military spokesmen say.
Their sole mission is to evacuate foreigners and the four governments all deny they will intervene to keep order.

The rebellion in Zaire, launched last October, has divided the Western allies with French and some Belgian officials joining Mobutu's people in accusing the United States and Britain of backing Kabila from the outset.

Mobutu's spokesman said the president would travel to Gabon on Wednesday for talks with leaders of six regional states, five of them strong allies of former colonial power France. Mobutu would return to Kinshasa on Friday.
The policy divergence is clear in the lack of a joint command and control of what each country stresses is not a multi-national task force.
South African President Nelson Mandela has not abandoned his mediation since hosting the first Mobutu-Kabila meeting held aboard a South African navy ship in Congo last Sunday.
The 90-minute session ended in failure with a communique that showed Mobutu refused to quit quietly and Kabila rejected a ceasefire.

The ailing president's camp believes if it can buy a few weeks' respite, ethnic cracks will appear in Kabila's motley alliance and residents of the capital will start to buy the argument that they could be replacing a former dictator they know with a new one they don't.
In an acute irony, the president's entourage is portraying Mobutu as a sincere democrat who is willing to discuss any non-violent process leading to a political transition.
The "Mobutists" are also drawing some comfort from clear signs that Kabila's perceived arrogance and duplicity have angered both the United States and Mandela in the past week.
"There is no doubt that Kabila lost some powerful friends in the runup to the talks with Mobutu," said a senior diplomatic source close to the search for a peaceful settlement.
But these are slender straws and while Mobutu clutches to grasp them, Kabila's fighters are marching towards his citadel.
